# Part A: Adult acquired flatfoot (progressive collapsing foot deformity)

## 1. Terminology and anatomy
- **Adult acquired flatfoot deformity (AAFD)**, renamed **progressive collapsing foot deformity (PCFD)** (2020 consensus): **complex 3D deformity** with **hindfoot valgus, forefoot abduction (talonavicular uncoverage), forefoot varus (supination), medial column instability (collapse of the arch)**, and later **ankle valgus**.
- **Tibialis posterior (TP):** **strongest invertor; primary dynamic stabiliser of the medial longitudinal arch**; inserts mainly on the **navicular tuberosity** with slips to the cuneiforms, cuboid and metatarsal bases 2-4; **locks the transverse tarsal (Chopart) joint** (TN and CC axes become non-parallel: rigid lever for push-off); **antagonist: peroneus brevis**.
- **Hypovascular zone** of TP tendon: **behind and just distal to the medial malleolus** (degeneration site).
- **Static stabilisers:** **spring ligament (calcaneonavicular: superomedial part most important)**, **deltoid ligament (deep)**, **plantar fascia (windlass mechanism)**, **talocalcaneal interosseous ligament**.
- **Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (PTTD)** was the classic cause, but **spring ligament failure** is now recognised as central; TP failure is often secondary.

## 2. Causes
- **TP tendon degeneration (commonest in middle-aged obese women; hypertension, diabetes, steroid injections, seronegative arthropathy)**.
- **Others:** **inflammatory arthritis (RA)**, **trauma (TP laceration/rupture, Lisfranc injury)**, **neuropathic (Charcot)**, **tarsal coalition (adult presentation)**, **accessory navicular**, **degenerative TMT/naviculocuneiform arthritis**, **iatrogenic**.

## 3. Clinical evaluation
- **Medial ankle pain along the TP tendon** (early), **lateral sinus tarsi/subfibular impingement pain** (late: calcaneofibular impingement).
- **"Too many toes" sign** (**forefoot abduction seen from behind**).
- **Single-limb heel rise test**: **inability to perform / no heel inversion on heel rise** (**most sensitive test for TP dysfunction**); **double heel rise** to check flexibility (hindfoot inverts if flexible).
- **Flexibility of the hindfoot (subtalar)** and **forefoot (forefoot varus/supination: compensatory fixed or flexible)**: **assess forefoot position with the hindfoot held in neutral**.
- **Gastrocnemius/Achilles contracture** (**Silfverskiöld test**: almost universal).
- **Medial column instability** (first TMT/naviculocuneiform plantar sag), **deltoid laxity (ankle valgus)**.

## 4. Imaging
- **Weight-bearing radiographs (AP and lateral foot, AP ankle, hindfoot alignment view (Saltzman))**:
  - **Lateral talo-first metatarsal angle (Meary angle): normal 0 degrees (collinear)**; **over 4 degrees convex plantar = flatfoot** (**mild 4-15, moderate 15-30, severe over 30**),
  - **Calcaneal pitch angle (normal about 20-30 degrees; reduced in flatfoot)**,
  - **AP talonavicular coverage angle (over 7 degrees) / talonavicular uncoverage percentage (over 40%)**: forefoot abduction,
  - **AP talo-first metatarsal angle** (**abduction**),
  - **Medial cuneiform-floor height** (reduced), **sinus tarsi impingement**, **subfibular impingement**.
  - **Ankle: talar tilt (valgus) in the mortise** (deltoid failure).
- **Weight-bearing CT** (**3D, subfibular impingement, middle facet subluxation**: **peritalar subluxation**).
- **MRI** (TP tendon tears/tendinosis, spring ligament), **ultrasound**.

## 5. Classification
### Johnson and Strom (modified by Myerson/Bluman)
| Stage | TP tendon | Hindfoot | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | **Tenosynovitis/tendinosis; normal length** | **Normal alignment; can single heel rise** (painful) | **Non-operative (immobilisation, NSAIDs, orthoses)**; **tenosynovectomy** |
| **II** (A/B/C) | **Elongated/dysfunctional** | **Flexible flatfoot** (**IIA mild abduction; IIB abduction over 30-40% TN uncoverage; IIC fixed forefoot varus**) | **Joint-sparing reconstruction**: **FDL transfer to the navicular + medializing calcaneal osteotomy (MDCO) ± lateral column lengthening (Evans) ± Cotton osteotomy ± gastrocnemius recession ± spring ligament repair** |
| **III** | **Ruptured/degenerated** | **Rigid flatfoot (fixed hindfoot valgus)** | **Triple arthrodesis** (or **double/modified: TN + subtalar**) |
| **IV** (A/B) | | **+ ankle valgus (deltoid failure)**: **IVA flexible (correctable), IVB rigid (tibiotalar arthritis)** | **IVA: deltoid reconstruction + hindfoot correction**; **IVB: tibiotalocalcaneal (TTC) or pantalar arthrodesis, or TAR + hindfoot correction** |
### PCFD consensus classification (2020)
- **Stage 1 (flexible) or 2 (rigid)**, with **classes A (hindfoot valgus), B (midfoot/forefoot abduction), C (forefoot varus/medial column instability), D (peritalar subluxation/dislocation), E (ankle instability: valgus)**; each scored as flexible or rigid.

## 6. Treatment details
- **Non-operative (all stages first, mainstay in elderly/low demand):** **CAM boot or short leg cast (acute tenosynovitis, 4-8 weeks)**, **orthoses (medial arch support + medial heel wedge; UCBL)**, **ankle-foot orthosis (Arizona brace)** for later stages, **physiotherapy (eccentric TP strengthening, Achilles stretching)**, weight loss. **Avoid steroid injection into the TP tendon sheath (rupture)**.
- **Flexible deformity (stage II) procedures:**
  - **FDL transfer to the navicular** (**FDL is in phase with and adjacent to the TP; weaker (about 30%) but adequate when combined with bony correction**; **FHL** alternative; **interconnection (Henry knot) allows the FHL to flex lesser toes**),
  - **Medializing displacement calcaneal osteotomy (MDCO)** (**about 10 mm medial shift**: **converts the Achilles tendon pull into an invertor (medial to the subtalar axis)**; **protects the tendon transfer**; **sural nerve and lateral calcaneal branch at risk; the tibial nerve/tarsal tunnel at risk with large shifts**),
  - **Lateral column lengthening (Evans osteotomy: anterior calcaneus between the anterior and middle facets, about 10-15 mm from the CC joint; or CC distraction arthrodesis)** for **forefoot abduction (TN uncoverage over about 40%)**: **lateral column overload (lateral foot pain: commonest complication)**, **CC arthritis**, **sural nerve injury**, non-union,
  - **Cotton osteotomy (plantarflexion opening-wedge osteotomy of the medial cuneiform)** or **first TMT arthrodesis (Lapidus)** for **residual forefoot varus/medial column instability**,
  - **Spring ligament repair/reconstruction**,
  - **Gastrocnemius recession (Strayer) / Achilles lengthening (Hoke)** for equinus,
  - **Subtalar arthroereisis** (sinus tarsi implant: limited role in adults; mainly paediatric).
- **Rigid deformity (stage III):** **triple arthrodesis (subtalar, TN, CC)** through **medial and lateral incisions (or single medial incision: protects lateral skin)**; **TN joint is the key joint (fusion of TN alone eliminates almost all hindfoot motion)**; **position: hindfoot about 5 degrees valgus, neutral forefoot rotation (plantigrade), neutral abduction**; **complications: non-union (TN commonest site), malunion, adjacent joint arthritis (ankle, naviculocuneiform)**.
- **Stage IV:** **deltoid ligament reconstruction** (flexible) or **TTC/pantalar arthrodesis** (rigid with arthritis); **total ankle replacement with hindfoot realignment**.

# Part B: Pes cavus

## 7. Definition and causes
- **Elevated medial longitudinal arch (high arch), often with hindfoot varus**; **forefoot-driven (plantarflexed first ray) or hindfoot-driven**.
- **About two-thirds have an underlying neurological cause**: **Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (HMSN type I: commonest; autosomal dominant; PMP22 duplication on chromosome 17p)**, **spinal cord pathology (tethered cord, diastematomyelia, syringomyelia, tumour, spinal dysraphism)**, **cerebral palsy**, **poliomyelitis (India: residual polio)**, **Friedreich ataxia**, **stroke**, **muscular dystrophy**. **Also:** **idiopathic/familial (subtle cavovarus)**, **residual clubfoot**, **trauma (compartment syndrome: Volkmann's ischaemic contracture: claw toes; malunited talar neck fracture)**.
- **Unilateral cavus = spinal cord lesion until proved otherwise: MRI whole spine.** **Bilateral cavus: think CMT (nerve conduction studies, genetic testing)**.

## 8. CMT pathomechanics
- **Muscle imbalance (pairs of agonist/antagonist; weakest muscles first: tibialis anterior and peroneus brevis; intrinsics):**
  - **Weak tibialis anterior vs strong peroneus longus**: **plantarflexed first ray (forefoot pronation/valgus)**,
  - **Weak peroneus brevis vs strong tibialis posterior**: **hindfoot varus, forefoot adduction**,
  - **Intrinsic weakness**: **claw toes** (**EDL recruited to dorsiflex the ankle: hyperextends MTPJs**),
  - **Plantar fascia contracture** (windlass: elevates the arch).
- **Tripod effect**: **plantarflexed first ray forces the hindfoot into varus on weight bearing (forefoot-driven hindfoot varus)**.
- **Lateral ankle instability, peroneal tendon tears, fifth metatarsal stress fractures, lateral foot callosities, stress fractures, ankle arthritis (varus)**.

## 9. Evaluation
- **Peek-a-boo heel sign** (**medial heel pad visible from the front with the feet parallel: hindfoot varus**).
- **Coleman block test** (**block under the lateral foot (heel and lateral forefoot), allowing the first ray to drop off the edge**): **hindfoot varus corrects = flexible hindfoot, deformity is forefoot-driven** (treat the forefoot: **first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy + plantar fascia release**); **does not correct = fixed hindfoot varus (needs calcaneal osteotomy or arthrodesis)**.
- **Muscle power testing** (MRC grading of each muscle: guides tendon transfers), **neurological examination** (reflexes, sensation, spine), **calluses (under first and fifth metatarsal heads)**.
- **Radiographs:** **Meary angle (talo-first metatarsal) convex dorsally (negative: over -4 degrees = cavus)**, **calcaneal pitch angle increased (over 30 degrees: calcaneocavus)**, **Hibbs angle** (calcaneus axis vs first metatarsal axis: **under 150 degrees** = cavus), **"double talar dome"** (ankle AP/lateral: hindfoot varus/external rotation), **fibula posterior**.

## 10. Treatment
- **Non-operative:** **orthoses (lateral forefoot post + recess under the first metatarsal head)**, **lateral heel wedge** (for flexible hindfoot), **AFO** (foot drop), **physiotherapy**, **footwear**.
- **Operative (individualised; "flexible deformities need soft-tissue/tendon procedures, fixed deformities need bony procedures, arthrodesis for severe rigid deformity or arthritis"):**
  - **Soft tissue:** **plantar fascia release (Steindler)**, **gastrocnemius recession/Achilles lengthening** (**in calcaneocavus (polio/spina bifida) the Achilles is weak: do not lengthen**).
  - **Tendon transfers (balance forces):** **peroneus longus to peroneus brevis transfer** (**removes plantarflexion of the first ray; augments eversion**), **tibialis posterior transfer to the dorsum (through the interosseous membrane to the lateral cuneiform)** for **foot drop**, **Jones transfer (EHL to the first metatarsal neck + hallux IPJ fusion)** for **clawed hallux**, **Hibbs transfer (EDL to the lateral cuneiform/cuboid)** for **claw lesser toes**, **flexor-to-extensor transfer (Girdlestone-Taylor)** for flexible claw toes.
  - **Bony (joint-sparing):** **dorsiflexion closing-wedge osteotomy of the first metatarsal base** (**forefoot-driven cavus**), **lateral closing-wedge calcaneal osteotomy (Dwyer)** or **lateralising calcaneal (Z) osteotomy** (**fixed hindfoot varus**), **midfoot osteotomy (Cole: dorsal closing wedge through the navicular-cuneiform/cuboid; Japas V-osteotomy; Akron dome)** for **midfoot cavus**, **anterior tibial osteotomy** rarely.
  - **Arthrodesis:** **triple arthrodesis** (**rigid deformity, arthritis, salvage**; **worse long-term results in CMT (ankle/midfoot arthritis)**: **avoid when possible in young patients**).
  - **Lateral ankle ligament reconstruction** (Broström) **must be combined with correction of the varus** (otherwise fails).

## 11. Paediatric flatfoot (brief link)
- **Flexible flatfoot: physiological; no treatment unless painful + tight heel cord (calcaneal lengthening + gastrocnemius recession)**.
- **Rigid flatfoot: tarsal coalition, CVT, accessory navicular, inflammatory, neuromuscular**: see paediatric foot notes.

## 12. Other conditions
- **Tibialis anterior tendon rupture:** **elderly men (sixth-seventh decade)**, **degenerative**, **foot slap/steppage gait**, **palpable gap/mass at the anterior ankle**, **EHL/EDL substitution (toe clawing on dorsiflexion)**; **repair/reconstruction (EHL transfer, graft) in active patients**; **AFO in low-demand**.
- **Accessory navicular (os naviculare)** in adults: **Kidner procedure (excision + TP advancement)**.
- **Tarsal tunnel syndrome:** **tibial nerve compression beneath the flexor retinaculum (laciniate ligament)**; **space-occupying lesions (ganglion, varicosities, lipoma, accessory muscles: flexor digitorum accessorius longus)**, **hindfoot valgus (traction)**, trauma; **burning plantar paraesthesia (sparing the heel (calcaneal branch arises proximal) in some cases), Tinel sign, dorsiflexion-eversion test**; **NCS**; **MRI**; **decompression (release of the flexor retinaculum + abductor hallucis fascia (medial and lateral plantar nerve tunnels))**: **results less predictable than CTS (about 50-75%)**, best with a **space-occupying lesion**.
- **Baxter nerve (first branch of the lateral plantar nerve / inferior calcaneal nerve) entrapment**: **chronic heel pain (medial)** mimicking plantar fasciitis; **abductor digiti minimi atrophy on MRI**; decompression with plantar fascia release.
- **Plantar fasciitis (heel pain):** **degenerative fasciosis at the medial calcaneal tubercle origin**; **first-step morning pain (post-static dyskinesia)**; **calcaneal spur (in FDB origin) is incidental**; **non-operative (about 90%: plantar fascia-specific stretching (best), Achilles stretching, heel cups, night splints, NSAIDs)**; **steroid injection (risk of fat pad atrophy and plantar fascia rupture)**, **ESWT**; **surgery (partial plantar fascia release (medial third to half: avoid complete release: lateral column overload)** ± **Baxter nerve release, gastrocnemius recession)** after **6-12 months**.

> Exam pearl: **PCFD/AAFD: TP + spring ligament failure; too many toes; can't single-heel-rise (most sensitive). Johnson-Strom: I tendinosis (conservative), II flexible (FDL transfer + MDCO ± Evans ± Cotton ± gastroc recession), III rigid (triple arthrodesis), IV ankle valgus (deltoid recon or TTC/TAR). MDCO converts Achilles to an invertor; Evans = lateral column overload.**

> Exam pearl: **Meary angle: plantar convex = flatfoot, dorsal convex = cavus. Calcaneal pitch high = calcaneocavus. TN joint key to triple arthrodesis (TN non-union commonest); position 5 degrees valgus.**

> Exam pearl: **Cavus: unilateral = spinal MRI; bilateral = CMT (PMP22). CMT: weak TA vs strong PL (plantarflexed first ray), weak PB vs strong TP (varus). Coleman block: corrects = forefoot-driven (first MT dorsiflexion osteotomy + plantar fascia release + PL to PB); does not correct = add Dwyer/lateralising calcaneal osteotomy. Jones transfer for clawed hallux. Broström fails without varus correction.**

> Exam pearl: **Tarsal tunnel: flexor retinaculum, space-occupying lesion gives best release results. Plantar fasciitis: stretching best; partial release only. Baxter nerve: ADM atrophy.**

hallux valgus and forefoot.md:
# Part A: Hallux valgus

## 1. Definition and aetiology
- **Lateral deviation of the hallux at the first MTPJ with medial deviation of the first metatarsal (metatarsus primus varus)**, with a medial prominence ("bunion").
- **Women (about 10:1 in surgical series)**, **familial (about 60-90% of juvenile cases; maternal transmission)**, **constricting footwear (narrow toe box, high heels)**, **ligamentous laxity**, **pes planus**, **first ray hypermobility (debated)**, **long first metatarsal**, **rounded metatarsal head**, **increased DMAA**, **inflammatory arthritis (RA)**, **neuromuscular (cerebral palsy, stroke)**, **amputation of the second toe**.

## 2. Pathoanatomy (sequence)
1. **Medial capsule and medial sesamoid ligament attenuation**; **the hallux drifts laterally (valgus)** pulled by **adductor hallucis** and the lateral pull of the **EHL and FHL** (**bowstring effect: become deforming forces**).
2. **The metatarsal head drifts medially off the sesamoids** (the **sesamoids stay in place: anchored by the adductor hallucis and the transverse metatarsal ligament**): **apparent lateral sesamoid displacement** relative to the metatarsal head; **crista erosion**.
3. **Pronation (eversion) of the hallux** (abductor hallucis migrates plantarly: loses abduction power; becomes a flexor/pronator).
4. **Lateral capsule and adductor contracture**; **transfer metatarsalgia** under the second metatarsal head (first ray loses load-bearing).
5. **Second toe deformities** (crossover toe, hammer toe), **second MTPJ instability/plantar plate tear**.

## 3. Evaluation
- **Weight-bearing AP and lateral radiographs** (and sesamoid axial view).
- **Normal values and severity:**
| Angle | Normal | Mild | Moderate | Severe |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Hallux valgus angle (HVA: first MT axis vs proximal phalanx axis)** | **Under 15 degrees** | **15-20** (up to 20-25 in some schemes) | **20-40** | **Over 40** |
| **Intermetatarsal angle (IMA: 1st-2nd MT)** | **Under 9 degrees** | **9-11** (under 13) | **11-16** (13-20) | **Over 16** (over 20) |
| **Distal metatarsal articular angle (DMAA)** | **Under 10 degrees** (about 6-10) | | | |
| **Hallux valgus interphalangeus (HVI)** | **Under 10 degrees** | | | |
- **Congruent vs incongruent joint:** **congruent (articular surfaces parallel; increased DMAA; juvenile)** vs **incongruent (subluxed: lateral subluxation of the phalanx on the head)**. **Congruent deformity: correction must not be done by soft-tissue release alone (would create an incongruent joint): use DMAA-correcting osteotomy (biplanar chevron) or extra-articular (double/triple) osteotomies**.
- **Sesamoid position (Hardy and Clapham: grades 1-7)**, **first MTPJ arthritis** (**hallux rigidus: fusion instead**), **first TMT hypermobility** (**dorsal translation over about 8-10 mm: Lapidus**), **metatarsus adductus** (**increased difficulty; IMA underestimated**), **pronation of the first metatarsal (round lateral head sign)**.

## 4. Management
### Non-operative
- **Wide toe-box footwear, bunion pads, orthoses, toe spacers**; **do not correct the deformity**; **surgery is for pain, not cosmesis** ("**never operate for cosmesis**").
### Operative principles: choose by severity, joint congruency, arthritis and TMT stability
| Deformity | Procedure | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Mild (HVA under 30, IMA under 13), congruent or incongruent** | **Distal metatarsal osteotomy: Chevron (Austin)** (**V-shaped osteotomy at the metatarsal head, apex distal; lateral shift up to about 30-50% of the head width**) ± **distal soft-tissue procedure (lateral release)** | **AVN of the metatarsal head** (**lateral release + chevron: avoid excessive dorsolateral dissection: nutrient vessels enter dorsolaterally (first dorsal metatarsal artery) and plantar-laterally**); **biplanar chevron for increased DMAA** |
| **Moderate (HVA 30-40, IMA 13-20)** | **Scarf osteotomy** (**Z-shaped diaphyseal osteotomy**: lateral translation; **troughing (fragments telescope into each other: elevation of the head, loss of height)**), **proximal metatarsal osteotomy (proximal chevron, crescentic, opening/closing wedge, Ludloff, Mau)** + **distal soft-tissue release** (modified McBride) | **Proximal osteotomies: more powerful correction (each degree of correction at the base produces more displacement distally)**; **dorsal malunion (elevatus: transfer metatarsalgia)** |
| **Severe (HVA over 40, IMA over 20)** | **Proximal osteotomy + distal soft-tissue procedure**, **Lapidus (first TMT arthrodesis)** | |
| **First TMT hypermobility / generalised laxity / recurrent HV** | **Modified Lapidus (first TMT arthrodesis)** | **Non-union (about 5-10%)**, **shortening (transfer metatarsalgia)**, dorsiflexion malunion |
| **Arthritis of the first MTPJ, severe deformity, neuromuscular, RA, salvage of failed surgery** | **First MTPJ arthrodesis** | **Position: about 10-15 degrees valgus, about 10-15 degrees dorsiflexion relative to the floor (about 20-25 degrees relative to the first metatarsal shaft), neutral rotation**; **IMA corrects spontaneously** after fusion |
| **Hallux valgus interphalangeus** | **Akin osteotomy** (**medial closing-wedge osteotomy of the proximal phalanx**) | Adjunct to other osteotomies |
| **Elderly, low-demand** | **Keller resection arthroplasty** (**excision of the base of the proximal phalanx**) | **Cock-up deformity, transfer metatarsalgia, weakness of push-off**; largely abandoned |
| **Juvenile/adolescent** | **Delay until skeletal maturity** (**high recurrence**); **guided growth (lateral hemiepiphysiodesis of the first metatarsal)** | **Increased DMAA common** |
- **Simple bunionectomy (Silver) alone**: **high recurrence; not used alone**.
- **McBride procedure** (original): **excision of the lateral sesamoid** (**hallux varus risk**), **adductor tenotomy**, **medial capsulorrhaphy**: **modified McBride = lateral release without sesamoid excision**.
- **Minimally invasive (MIS) third/fourth generation (MICA/percutaneous chevron-Akin)**: increasingly used; similar outcomes; learning curve.

## 5. Complications
- **Recurrence (commonest; about 10-25%)**: **undercorrection of the IMA**, **unrecognised increased DMAA**, **unaddressed pronation**, **first TMT hypermobility**, **juvenile**, **poor sesamoid reduction**.
- **Hallux varus** (**overcorrection: excessive lateral release, lateral sesamoid excision, excessive medial eminence resection (staking the sagittal sulcus), overtightened medial capsule, IMA overcorrection (negative)**): **flexible: EHB tenodesis/EHL transfer; rigid/arthritic: MTPJ fusion**.
- **AVN of the metatarsal head** (**chevron + extensive lateral release**).
- **Transfer metatarsalgia** (**shortening or dorsal malunion of the first metatarsal**).
- **Stiffness of the first MTPJ**, **non-union/malunion**, **infection**, **dorsomedial cutaneous nerve injury (neuroma)** (**medial dorsal cutaneous branch of the superficial peroneal nerve**), **CRPS**.

# Part B: Hallux rigidus

## 6. Hallux rigidus (first MTPJ OA)
- **Commonest arthritis of the foot**; **dorsal osteophyte (dorsal bunion)** limiting **dorsiflexion (pain at push-off)**; **positive grind test (late)**; **adolescent form (OCD of the metatarsal head)**.
- **Coughlin and Shurnas classification (grades 0-4):** **0 stiffness, normal radiograph**; **1 mild, dorsal osteophyte, preserved joint space**; **2 moderate, joint space narrowing, pain at extremes**; **3 severe, under 10-20% residual motion, pain at extremes, more narrowing**; **4: as 3 with pain in mid-range (positive grind test)**.
- **Treatment:**
  - **Non-operative:** **stiff-soled shoe, rocker sole, Morton's extension (carbon plate)**, NSAIDs, steroid injection.
  - **Cheilectomy** (**excision of the dorsal osteophyte and dorsal 25-30% of the metatarsal head**): **grades 1-2 (and selected 3)**; **pain at the extremes, not mid-range**; **± Moberg osteotomy (dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy of the proximal phalanx: shifts the arc into dorsiflexion)**.
  - **First MTPJ arthrodesis**: **gold standard for grades 3-4** (**predictable pain relief**; **position: 10-15 degrees dorsiflexion relative to the floor, 10-15 degrees valgus, neutral rotation**).
  - **Interpositional arthroplasty/Keller** (elderly), **hemiarthroplasty (synthetic cartilage implant, Cartiva: mixed results)**; **silicone/total joint arthroplasty: high failure (silicone synovitis, subsidence)**.

# Part C: Lesser toe deformities and forefoot pain

## 7. Lesser toe deformities
| Deformity | MTPJ | PIPJ | DIPJ | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Mallet toe** | Neutral | Neutral | **Flexed** | **FDL contracture** |
| **Hammer toe** | **Neutral or slightly extended** | **Flexed** | **Neutral/extended** | **Commonest; second toe**; FDL/FDB contracture |
| **Claw toe** | **Hyperextended** | **Flexed** | **Flexed** | **Usually multiple toes, bilateral: neuromuscular (CMT, diabetes neuropathy), RA, cavus foot**: **intrinsic weakness** (lumbrical/interossei) |
| **Curly toe** | | Flexed + varus (rotated) | | **Congenital** (FDL tightness) |
- **Flexible deformities: flexor-to-extensor transfer (Girdlestone-Taylor: FDL split to the extensor hood/dorsum of the proximal phalanx)**, **FDL tenotomy (mallet)**.
- **Fixed deformities: PIPJ resection arthroplasty (DuVries) or PIPJ arthrodesis**; **MTPJ: extensor tendon lengthening (EDL Z-lengthening), EDB tenotomy, dorsal capsulotomy**; **Weil osteotomy** (**oblique shortening osteotomy of the metatarsal neck**: for **MTPJ dislocation/subluxation, long metatarsal**: **floating toe** = commonest complication).
- **Crossover second toe / second MTPJ instability (plantar plate tear):** **dorsomedial drift of the second toe**, **pain under the second MTPJ**, **positive drawer (Lachman) test of the MTPJ**; **Coughlin plantar plate grading**; **plantar plate repair + Weil osteotomy**, flexor-to-extensor transfer.
- **Freiberg disease** (second metatarsal head osteochondrosis: adolescent girls; dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy).

## 8. Metatarsalgia
- **Pain under the metatarsal heads**: **primary** (**long second metatarsal**, plantarflexed metatarsal, **cavus foot**, prominent condyles), **secondary** (**inflammatory arthritis, Freiberg, MTPJ synovitis, gastrocnemius tightness**), **iatrogenic (transfer after hallux valgus surgery)**.
- **Intractable plantar keratosis (IPK)**: **discrete** (beneath a prominent fibular condyle) vs **diffuse** (beneath a long metatarsal).
- **Gastrocnemius contracture (positive Silfverskiöld test: ankle dorsiflexion limited with the knee extended, improves with the knee flexed)**: **gastrocnemius recession (Strayer)**.
- **Treatment:** **metatarsal pad (placed proximal to the metatarsal heads)**, rocker-bottom sole, orthoses; **Weil osteotomy**, **condylectomy**.

## 9. Morton neuroma (interdigital neuroma)
- **Perineural fibrosis of the common digital nerve** (**not a true neuroma**), **distal to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament**; **third web space (between 3rd and 4th metatarsal heads) commonest**, then second; **women (about 5-10:1)**, **narrow/high-heeled shoes**.
- **Burning plantar forefoot pain radiating into the toes**, **numbness**, **"walking on a pebble"**; **Mulder click (squeezing the forefoot mediolaterally while pressing the web space)**, **web space tenderness**; **splaying of the toes (Sullivan sign)**.
- **Imaging: ultrasound or MRI** (size **over about 5 mm**); **differentials: MTPJ synovitis/plantar plate tear (second web), stress fracture, intermetatarsal bursitis, tarsal tunnel syndrome, lumbar radiculopathy**.
- **Treatment:** **wide shoes, metatarsal pad, steroid injection (up to about 50-80% relief)**, **alcohol sclerosing injections**, **radiofrequency ablation**; **surgery: neurectomy (dorsal approach preferred: avoids plantar scar; divide the deep transverse metatarsal ligament; resect the nerve proximal to the ligament, about 3 cm)** (**about 80-90% success**); **recurrent (stump) neuroma (about 5-10%)**: **plantar approach** for revision; **decompression (ligament release) alone** as an alternative.

## 10. Sesamoid disorders
- **Sesamoiditis, stress fracture, AVN, osteochondritis, OA, bipartite sesamoid (medial/tibial sesamoid commonest: about 10-30%; bilateral in about 85%: compare with the other foot)**, **turf toe**.
- **Turf toe:** **hyperdorsiflexion injury of the first MTPJ (plantar plate/capsuloligamentous complex)**: **American football on artificial turf**; **grade I** sprain, **II** partial tear, **III** complete tear (**proximal migration of sesamoids**, **sesamoid diastasis**, **vertical instability: Lachman positive**); **grade III: surgical repair** of the plantar plate.
- **Treatment of sesamoid pain:** offloading (dancer's pad, orthoses), boot/cast; **sesamoidectomy** (refractory: **excision of both sesamoids causes cock-up deformity: avoid**; **medial sesamoid excision: hallux valgus**; **lateral sesamoid excision: hallux varus**).

## 11. Bunionette (tailor's bunion)
- **Lateral prominence of the fifth metatarsal head**; **Coughlin types:** **I enlarged/prominent head**, **II lateral bowing of the fifth metatarsal**, **III increased 4-5 intermetatarsal angle (over 8-10 degrees: commonest symptomatic)**.
- **Treatment:** **wide shoes**; **type I: lateral condylectomy** or **distal chevron osteotomy**; **type II: distal chevron or diaphyseal (oblique/scarf) osteotomy**; **type III: diaphyseal oblique or proximal osteotomy** (**proximal fifth metatarsal osteotomy: poor blood supply: non-union**).

> Exam pearl: **HVA under 15 and IMA under 9 normal; DMAA under 10. Sesamoids stay; the metatarsal head drifts medially. Congruent joint (increased DMAA, juvenile) needs DMAA-correcting osteotomy, not soft-tissue release. Mild: chevron; moderate: scarf/proximal osteotomy; severe/hypermobile: Lapidus; arthritic: fusion (10-15 valgus, 10-15 dorsiflexion to floor). Commonest complication: recurrence; hallux varus = overcorrection (lateral sesamoid excision).**

> Exam pearl: **Hallux rigidus: Coughlin-Shurnas; cheilectomy for pain at the extremes (grade 1-2, ± Moberg); mid-range pain/grind (3-4) = fusion.**

> Exam pearl: **Claw toe (MTPJ hyperextension): neuromuscular/cavus; flexible: Girdlestone-Taylor (FDL to extensor). Crossover second toe = plantar plate tear (drawer test): repair + Weil (floating toe). Morton neuroma: 3rd web, Mulder click, distal to DTML; neurectomy via dorsal approach. Bunionette type III (increased 4-5 IMA) = diaphyseal osteotomy.**
